chunks: "For an ideal square wave the answer is: there isn't one. The edges are instantaneous, so the harmonics at 3f, 5f, 7f and so on keep going with amplitude one over n, forever.
You'd need infinite bandwidth to reproduce it. A real square wave has a finite rise time, and that changes the story.

Mathematically a trapezoid still has infinitely many harmonics, but above a knee frequency of roughly one over pi times the rise time the amplitudes fall like one over n squared, so 40 decibels per decade instead of 20.
Add the fact that real drivers, traces and packages are low-pass, and the content above a few times that knee is negligible, usually well below the noise floor or the emissions limit.
So I'd say the highest significant frequency component of a real square wave is set by the edge, not the clock: roughly 0. 35 to 0. 5 divided by the rise time.
A 100 megahertz clock with a 1 nanoseconds edge has important content out to about 350 to 500 megahertz, which is the 3rd to 5th harmonic.
And a 10 megahertz clock with a 100 picoseconds edge has content out to several GHz, which is why a slow clock can still wreck your EMI or need a fast scope."
